extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly; general educated public interested in natural science (biology and metrology)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository popular-science article explaining vertebrate circulation and standards/measures of length; intended to inform general readers about physiological differences across taxa and the practical/scientific requirements for standard measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed circulation in vertebrates
rubrics_metrics.description: In vertebrates alone is there a closed circulation — a complete system of tubes from whence the blood never escapes into the body-cavity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare with higher mollusks which show an approach to it; closed circulatory system of even the lowest vertebrates is of higher type and admits of great and curious modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three capillary systems
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist in vertebrates three sets of capillary blood-vessels, usually spoken of as three systems: the body/systemic circulation, the respiratory/pulmonary circulation, and the liver/portal circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although distinguished, together they constitute a single circuit; lymphatic circulation is connected by the thoracic duct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lymphatic system function and distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The lymphatics collect the waste matter of the tissues and return it to the blood to be again used or excreted; lymph is colorless and contains corpuscles resembling white blood corpuscles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lymphatics are minute capillary vessels found in all parts of the vertebrate body except perhaps the bulb of the eye, cartilages, and bones; lacteals are modified lymphatics for chyle; valves keep lymph flowing toward larger trunks; lymphatics may form glands (thymus, thyroid, spleen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heart structure in fishes
rubrics_metrics.description: Fishes have a heart resembling that of the mollusks: a double force-pump consisting of a receiving-chamber (auricle) and a propelling-chamber (ventricle), with valves to prevent backward flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fish heart is respiratory — it sends blood directly to breathing organs (gills) so it passes only impure blood to gills; after gill purification blood passes through systemic and portal capillaries back to heart without further propulsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessory/primitive circulatory mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Some low vertebrates or chordates lack a special heart or have auxiliary hearts or contractile venous bulbs (e.g., amphioxus has contractile bulbs; eel has auxiliary heart in tail; hag aided by contractility of portal vein).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some lower animals lymphatic tubes assume large sinuses and connect with veins; lymphatic hearts occur in frogs (four sinuses with muscular walls).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed circulation in amphibians and many reptiles
rubrics_metrics.description: Amphibians and many reptiles have one ventricle for two auricles, so pure blood from breathing organs and impure blood from the body are mingled, resulting in mixed blood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This arrangement reduces body temperature compared to 'warm-blooded' animals; complex heart parts and valves prevent complete mixing though not perfect separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial separation of ventricles in reptiles
rubrics_metrics.description: Reptilian ventricles are more or less divided by a membranous partition; partition is perfect only in the crocodile where right and left ventricles have no communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with structural partition, in many reptiles some mingling persists via arterial communications near origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-chambered heart in birds and mammals
rubrics_metrics.description: Birds and mammals have two auricles and two ventricles; the right and left sides of the heart are entirely distinct and functionally act as two hearts (systemic and pulmonary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pure and impure blood never mingle; all blood passes through lungs and is oxygenated every circuit; embryonic foramen ovale is normally closed later, persistent opening reduces physiology to reptilian condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pericardium and unified heart beating
rubrics_metrics.description: The two functional 'hearts' (right and left halves) are formed of the same circular muscles and enclosed by the lubricating membrane called the pericardium; their contraction/dilation in unison produces the 'beating' of the heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First heart sound uncertain but occurs at ventricle contraction; second sound produced on ventricular dilation by flapping back of semilunar valves at artery origins to prevent regurgitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulatory power and work estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: The heart performs enormous work; human blood volume is at least six quarts and completes circulation in about thirty-two heart-beats; estimated hourly and daily mechanical work comparisons are provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives comparative examples (engine/lifter/climber) and daily work estimate (seventy-five thousand kilogramme-metres) to illustrate power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branching geometry and flow characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Arteries branch at acute angles facilitating successive impulses; veins branch at greater angles compatible with steady and slower flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because veins carry same blood amount more slowly they have greater diameter/capacity; branching geometry facilitates pulsatile arterial flow vs steady venous flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure gradient from heart
rubrics_metrics.description: Blood pressure diminishes from the heart; in the carotid artery of man pressure probably equals weight of 150 to 200 cubic millimetres of mercury; pulmonary artery pressure only 30 to 40 cubic millimetres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Values are indicative and subject to experimental disagreement; overall point is gradual diminution of pressure with distance from heart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Velocity of blood varies by species and vessel size
rubrics_metrics.description: Blood velocity differs across species and vessels (e.g., horse carotid ~300 mm/s; dog 300–500 mm/s; human large arteries hardly over 20 inches/s; capillary length ~0.5 mm and blood passes in about 1 second).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Velocity decreases from ventricles toward capillaries then increases from capillaries toward auricles; capillaries' large total sectional area delays blood for intimate tissue contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capillary wall permeability
rubrics_metrics.description: Walls of capillaries are of extreme tenuity and easily permeable under osmosis; even corpuscles can pass outward through the walls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to allow intimate exchange between blood and tissues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arterial elasticity aids continuous flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Elasticity of arteries increases carrying capacity; arteries expand under each heart-contraction then contract, helping onward flow — serving the same purpose as an air-chamber in a force-pump.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elasticity equalizes the flow and increases amount delivered; whole driving force derived from heart, arteries help maintain continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veins and venous return mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Veins are lax tubes larger than arteries, capable of holding large blood volume and conveying it more slowly; veins have valves preventing backward flow; compression from muscular contraction assists forward venous flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Movements such as chest breathing likely aid pulmonary circulation by assisting vacuum filling during inspiration; venous valves and muscle compression explain why exercise hastens circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tissue 'attraction' and nervous regulation of blood supply
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists an admitted force in capillaries resulting from attraction of tissues for arterial blood containing oxygen and nutriment; vital condition of tissue adapts blood amount to organ needs, while nervous system regulates supply by varying vessel caliber.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains local regulation (e.g., blushing as temporary capillary expansion; congestion as permanent expansion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collateral circulation and arterial protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Arteries are connected by branches or loops so that if circulation in a large artery stops, other vessels can expand over hours to carry sufficient blood; arteries are deep-seated and loop at joints to prevent stoppage by compression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include arterial protection by muscles and bone (e.g., lion's arm artery passing through bone perforation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulse rate correlates with activity and species
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapidity of circulation generally proportional to activity of the animal: bird pulse ~150/min, cat 115, dog 95, man 72, ox 35; exceptions exist (invertebrates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human pulse faster in childhood and old age, slightly faster evening than morning, faster in summer than winter, may increase with altitude; fever greatly quickens circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capillary sectional area purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Capillaries have a sectional area several times that of the aorta to delay blood at the time it is brought into most intimate contact with tissues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains the decrease in velocity toward capillaries and the requirement for slow transit to allow exchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: After-death movement of blood
rubrics_metrics.description: Some force in capillaries or other cause carries blood after death from the arteries into the veins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically significant: observation of empty arteries after death led to earlier misconception that arteries conveyed air; Harvey overturned this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessory hearts in other animals
rubrics_metrics.description: Some animals possess accessory hearts aiding circulation (e.g., rhythmic contraction of veins in bat wings; lymphatic hearts in frogs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower animals also may use body movements or cilia to effect circulation (e.g., jellyfish, anemone, sponge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards custody and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards of weight and extension (length) are of great practical importance and must be held in custody of national governments, scientific societies, and institutions so copies can be made to prevent gradual alteration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constant use wears measures; accepted standards allow uniform absolute values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of comparing measures and personal equation
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparing one measure with another is not simple; utmost skill, long experience, and elaborate/costly apparatus are required; allowance must be made for very small errors and for the observer's 'personal equation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Results by two observers with different instruments will probably not agree; personal equation has not yet been eliminated in such work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscope-based comparisons affected by magnification and illumination
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons of measures of length made with microscopes are affected by the magnification and by the method of illumination employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurements require careful support of the standard bar and control of optical conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support and anti-flexure requirements for standard bars
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard metal bars must be carefully supported on rollers mutually connected by a system of levers so no flexure can take place, or else placed on a bedplate adjusted in a horizontal plane so no effect of flexure is detected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Rogers' bedplate believed to have no part more than .00002 of an inch from true level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material and shape considerations for standards
rubrics_metrics.description: In constructing a standard the shape of the bar and the material of which it is composed require careful consideration; standards can undergo molecular change altering their length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a Russian iron standard shortened by about 1/6000 of an inch after transport ~8000 miles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperature effects and equilibration times
rubrics_metrics.description: Influence of temperature upon length of a metal bar is significant; if two steel bars (one nickel-plated) are subjected to gradual temperature change they acquire true length after ~12 hours; abrupt changes may require 48–60 hours before safe comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful measurements must allow sufficient time for thermal equilibration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and legal nature of yard/metre standards
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no natural unit from which the yard was derived; the imperial standard yard was legalized by Parliament and copies distributed; the French metre was originally defined as one ten-millionth of the quadrant of a meridian but later the Archives-metre was perpetuated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards often depend on historical/legal decisions rather than immutable natural units; awareness of provenance and legal status (e.g., US bronze bar No.11 used but not legislatively sanctioned) is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baily's metal composition for standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Baily proposed an alloy for standard measures composed of sixteen parts copper, two and a half parts tin, and one part zinc (known as Baily's metal); 'bronze 19' standard was made of this alloy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical properties (durability, stability) motivated alloy choice; 'bronze 19' legalized in 1855 and several copies distributed to institutions/governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: International metre decisions and prototype materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission Internationale du Metre decided to perpetuate the Archives-metre as true metre and later selected an iridio-platinum alloy for standards composed of ninety parts platinum and ten parts iridium with ±2% allowance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An International Bureau of Weights and Measures (1874) was established at Paris to care for prototype standards and construct/verify copies.
